text: Gene-level fitness correlations were positive in 311/317 organism-metal pair observations (98.1%); 99.1% were significant at p < 0.05. All 15 pairs tested in ≥5 organisms had >90% sign consistency.
quote: Across 317 organism-metal pair observations (28 organisms, 85 unique metal pairs), **98.1% of gene-level fitness correlations are positive** (311/317) and **99.1% are statistically significant** (p < 0.05). All 15 metal pairs tested in ≥5 organisms show >90% sign consistency — no metal pair has systematically negative cross-resistance in any organism.
heading: 1. Metal cross-resistance is universal and directionally conserved (H1 strongly supported)

text: Ni-Co cross-resistance had mean r = 0.56 across 28 organisms.
quote: - **Ni-Co** (r = 0.56, n = 28 organisms): The classic divalent cation cross-resistance pair, now validated at gene resolution across diverse phyla
heading: 1. Metal cross-resistance is universal and directionally conserved (H1 strongly supported)

text: Fe-Zn had mean r = 0.61 across 6 organisms; shared disruption of iron-sulfur cluster proteins is proposed as an explanation, not demonstrated.
quote: - **Fe-Zn** (r = 0.61, n = 6): Unexpectedly strong; likely reflects shared disruption of iron-sulfur cluster proteins
heading: 1. Metal cross-resistance is universal and directionally conserved (H1 strongly supported)

text: Cu-U had mean r = 0.51 across 5 organisms; the report links both metals to membrane/oxidative damage.

heading: 1. Metal cross-resistance is universal and directionally conserved (H1 strongly supported)

text: Al was the most independent metal, with mean r = 0.34; its trivalent toxicity mechanism is offered as an interpretation.
quote: - **Al** is the most independent metal (mean r = 0.34): Consistent with its unique trivalent toxicity mechanism
heading: 1. Metal cross-resistance is universal and directionally conserved (H1 strongly supported)

text: The report distinguishes broadly positive cross-resistance direction from only moderately conserved magnitude (leave-one-out r = 0.41; Mantel mean r = 0.23).
quote: The direction of cross-resistance (all positive) is universal; the quantitative magnitude is moderately conserved across organisms (leave-one-out consensus prediction r = 0.41, Mantel mean r = 0.23).
heading: 1. Metal cross-resistance is universal and directionally conserved (H1 strongly supported)

text: Across 28 organisms in four named phyla, Co-Ni had median r ≈ 0.58; Al-Co and Al-Ni had median r ≈ 0.30.
quote: The boxplot shows that for each metal pair, the distribution of Pearson r values across organisms is consistently positive, with tight interquartile ranges. Co-Ni (median r ≈ 0.58) is the strongest pair across 28 organisms spanning Proteobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, and Actinobacteria. Al-Co and Al-Ni are the weakest pairs (median r ≈ 0.30), consistent with aluminum's distinct toxicity mechanism.
heading: 2. Cross-resistance patterns are consistent across phylogenetically diverse organisms

text: Individual heatmaps showed positive cross-resistance, with the Ni-Co/Co-Zn block among the strongest; DvH covered 13 metals, with Mo most independent.
quote: Individual organism heatmaps show the same qualitative structure: warm colors throughout (positive cross-resistance), with the Ni-Co/Co-Zn block consistently among the strongest. DvH (13 metals) provides the richest single-organism view, with Mo standing out as the most independent metal.
heading: 2. Cross-resistance patterns are consistent across phylogenetically diverse organisms

text: Rankings of 10 common metal pairs across 12 organisms with ≥5 metals showed mostly positive pairwise Spearman agreement.
quote: Pairwise Spearman correlations between organism cross-resistance rankings (on the 10 common metal pairs across 12 organisms with ≥5 metals) show mostly positive agreement, confirming that organisms rank metal pairs similarly.
heading: 2. Cross-resistance patterns are consistent across phylogenetically diverse organisms

text: Mantel tests across 351 organism pairs had mean r = 0.23, with 62% positive.
quote: Mantel tests across 351 organism pairs show mean r = 0.23 with 62% positive — moderate but consistent conservation of cross-resistance architecture.
heading: 3. Conservation is validated by Mantel tests and LOO prediction, but the permutation test design requires nuance

text: The metal-label permutation test was non-significant (p = 0.42); the report cautions that uniformly positive correlations make the mean insensitive to label shuffling.
quote: The metal-label permutation test (p = 0.42) is non-significant because ALL metal pairs are positive; shuffling labels doesn't change the mean when correlations are uniformly positive.
heading: 3. Conservation is validated by Mantel tests and LOO prediction, but the permutation test design requires nuance

text: Leave-one-out consensus prediction had mean r = 0.41, but only 2/28 organisms reached individual significance.
quote: The leave-one-out consensus prediction (mean r = 0.41) shows that a universal cross-resistance map is a useful predictor of individual organism patterns, though only 2/28 organisms reach individual significance — indicating that the consensus captures the average trend but individual organisms have meaningful deviations.
heading: 3. Conservation is validated by Mantel tests and LOO prediction, but the permutation test design requires nuance

text: The analysis classified 8,162 metal-important genes across 28 organisms into three tiers.
quote: Metal-important genes (8,162 across 28 organisms) decompose into three tiers:
heading: 4. Three-tier gene architecture: general stress > metal-shared > metal-specific in core enrichment (H2 supported)

text: General-stress tier: 1,484 genes, 18.2% of metal-important genes, mean 92.0% core, and 57.2% fully core (≥95%).
heading: 4. Three-tier gene architecture: general stress > metal-shared > metal-specific in core enrichment (H2 supported)

text: Metal-shared tier: 2,306 genes, 28.3% of metal-important genes, mean 91.0% core, and 50.4% fully core (≥95%).
heading: 4. Three-tier gene architecture: general stress > metal-shared > metal-specific in core enrichment (H2 supported)

text: Metal-specific tier: 4,372 genes, 53.6% of metal-important genes, mean 89.8% core, and 45.7% fully core (≥95%).
heading: 4. Three-tier gene architecture: general stress > metal-shared > metal-specific in core enrichment (H2 supported)

text: Pangenome conservation declined from general-stress to metal-shared (important for ≥2 metals) to metal-specific (important for exactly 1 metal) genes; fully-core proportions were 57.2%, 50.4%, and 45.7%, an 11.5 percentage-point spread.
quote: The predicted gradient holds: general stress genes (pleiotropic, important across many conditions) are the most conserved in the pangenome, metal-shared genes (cross-resistance drivers, important for ≥2 metals) are intermediate, and metal-specific genes (important for exactly 1 metal) are least conserved. The "fully core" gradient (57.2% → 50.4% → 45.7%) is particularly clear — an 11.5 percentage point spread.
heading: 4. Three-tier gene architecture: general stress > metal-shared > metal-specific in core enrichment (H2 supported)

text: The report proposes an evolutionary model from ancestral general-stress defense through shared metal defense to specialized metal-specific resistance. Ancestry and evolutionary rates are interpretations, not directly demonstrated here.
quote: This supports the evolutionary model: **ancestral general stress defense** (deepest core) → **shared metal defense** (core, evolving slower) → **specialized metal-specific resistance** (more accessory, evolving faster).
heading: 4. Three-tier gene architecture: general stress > metal-shared > metal-specific in core enrichment (H2 supported)

text: Functional keyword analysis associated general-stress genes with energy/respiration and cell-envelope functions, and metal-specific genes with transporters/efflux and iron/metal-related functions.
quote: Functional keyword analysis shows that general stress genes are enriched for energy/respiration and cell envelope functions, while metal-specific genes are enriched for transporters/efflux and iron/metal-related functions — consistent with the expectation that specialized metal resistance is mediated by dedicated transport systems.
heading: 4. Three-tier gene architecture: general stress > metal-shared > metal-specific in core enrichment (H2 supported)

text: The report identified 318 metal-shared ortholog groups important for ≥2 metals in ≥2 organisms; the broadest spanned up to 14 organisms and included cell-envelope, energy-metabolism, DNA-repair, and ion-homeostasis functions.
quote: NB05 identified 318 ortholog groups (OGs) that are metal-shared (important for ≥2 metals) in ≥2 organisms. The most broadly conserved families span up to 14 organisms and encode cell envelope, energy metabolism, DNA repair, and ion homeostasis functions. These represent the core machinery of multi-metal tolerance — gene families that are consistently required for defense against multiple metals across phylogenetically diverse bacteria.

text: The report contrasts its underpowered validation with a prior pangenome-scale analysis of 42K strains (Cohen's d = +1.0) and proposes testing signatures across 27K species using KEGG/PFAM mapping.
quote: This null result is expected: the prior `bacdive_metal_validation` project demonstrated that metal tolerance prediction requires pangenome-scale analysis (42K strains, Cohen's d = +1.0) to achieve statistical power. A proper H3 test would need the KEGG/PFAM mapping approach from the Metal Fitness Atlas applied to the cross-resistance gene signatures across 27K species.

text: CzcCBA is a named efflux system linked here to Co-Ni-Zn cross-resistance; the report's genome-wide Co-Ni comparison had r = 0.56 across 28 organisms.
quote: - **Cross-resistance direction agrees with classical work**: Nies (1999, 2003) described Co-Ni-Zn cross-resistance mediated by CzcCBA efflux systems. Our gene-level data confirms this pair (r = 0.56, n = 28 organisms) and extends it to show that the *entire genome* responds similarly to Co and Ni — not just efflux genes.
heading: Literature Context

text: The Metal Fitness Atlas is a named prior project; this report contrasts its 87.4% core estimate for metal genes with the within-metal-gene tier gradient.
quote: - **Extends the Metal Fitness Atlas**: The Metal Fitness Atlas (this observatory) showed metal genes are 87.4% core. We now show that *within* metal genes, there's a finer gradient: general stress (92%) > shared (91%) > specific (90%) — the core enrichment is layered, reflecting the evolutionary history of metal tolerance.
heading: Literature Context

text: The report says the counter_ion_effects project found DvH's metal–NaCl correlation hierarchy followed toxicity mechanism rather than counter-ion identity, and interprets its metal–metal correlations across 28 organisms as showing similar mechanistic grouping.
quote: - **Counter ion effects validated**: The counter_ion_effects project (this observatory) showed that DvH's metal-NaCl correlation hierarchy follows toxicity mechanism, not counter ion identity. Our cross-resistance matrices confirm and extend this: the same mechanistic grouping emerges from metal-metal correlations across 28 organisms.
heading: Literature Context

text: Different metal concentrations across experiments may confound cross-resistance estimates through dose-response effects.
quote: - **Metal concentration variation**: Different experiments used different metal concentrations. Dose-response effects could influence cross-resistance estimates.

text: Organisms had 3 to 112 metal experiments, producing unequal reliability in per-organism matrices.
quote: - **Unequal experiment counts**: Organisms range from 3 to 112 metal experiments, affecting the reliability of per-organism matrices.
heading: Limitations

text: The 28 organisms are phylogenetically non-independent; phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS) or independent contrasts were not applied to strengthen the conservation claim.
quote: - **Phylogenetic non-independence**: The 28 organisms are not phylogenetically independent. Formal phylogenetic comparative methods (PGLS, independent contrasts) would strengthen the conservation claim.
heading: Limitations

text: The limitations section gives n = 26 at Fitness Browser organism scale, while the corrected species-level passage reports 20 independent species; these are distinct reported denominators.
quote: - **H3 underpowered**: BacDive validation at FB organism scale (n = 26) lacks the statistical power achieved by the Metal Fitness Atlas at pangenome scale (42K strains).
heading: Limitations

text: Without non-metal stress controls, the analysis cannot distinguish universal metal cross-resistance from general stress shared by all metals.
quote: - **No negative controls**: All tested metal pairs are positive. We cannot distinguish "universal cross-resistance" from "all metals cause general stress" without non-metal stress controls (partially addressed by the counter_ion_effects project).
